title: Remembering the Lost Chola Port of Poompuhar Through Cultural Architecture: Theera Ula, a Journey Through Land and Sea
content: Poompuhar, once a thriving port of the early Chola era in South India, now lies largely beneath the sea. Sangam literature describes markets, warehouses and a lighthouse on trade routes reaching the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia and China, but marine surveys have found only scattered remains offshore. The present town is a small coastal settlement battered by the 2004 tsunami. This project analysis asks how architecture can conserve heritage through spatial memory and living practice when the physical fabric is lost. It examines Theera Ula (தீரா உலா, "the timeless journey"), a socio-cultural centre proposed in a 2020 design thesis. The design followed an issue-led sequence: literary and archaeological evidence set the cultural brief, four precedents informed the spatial strategy, site analysis shaped the route, and conversations with fishermen, nadaswaram makers and locals defined the programme. The scheme gathers the site's surviving fragments, a temple, a memorial pillar and a lighthouse, into a descending route of thresholds from town to shore, ending at a boat deck above the submerged port. The paper argues that heritage without fabric is best conserved by connecting what remains and offers the issue-led sequence as a method for other coastal sites, while acknowledging that an unbuilt proposal cannot confirm these conclusions.
